name: Design a Package Registry
intent: Let millions of developers publish and install versioned packages, serve billions of downloads a day from a cache, and keep the whole chain safe from tampering, deletion and malicious uploads.
codeTitle: version ranges, immutable publishes and integrity checks
finalIntro: One publish, one install, and one bad package that is stopped.
prompt: Design a public package registry like npm or PyPI. Maintainers publish versions of a package, and every build in the world downloads packages and their dependencies by name and version range. A published version must never change, installs must be fast and must keep working, and the registry must resist stolen accounts, look-alike names and malware.
functional: Publish a new version of a package, with its tarball and metadata
Download the tarball for an exact name and version
Return the list of versions and their dependencies, so that a client can pick versions that satisfy ranges
Authenticate publishers, and show where and how a version was built
Yank or deprecate a bad version, and handle removal requests
Search packages, and warn about suspicious ones
nonFunctional: Handle about 10 billion downloads a day, with peaks of two to three times the average
A version is immutable: the same name and version always gives the same bytes
Installs are fast from anywhere, and a lockfile build keeps working through a registry outage
A new version is visible for installs within about a minute
Tampering by anyone, including a compromised mirror or CDN, is detectable by the client
Malware and look-alike names are caught early, with little friction for honest maintainers

firstAttempt.text: One web server with a database table of packages and a folder of tarballs. A publish uploads a file to the folder and inserts a row. An install downloads the file from the same server, and a client works out dependencies by calling the server once per package. The maintainer can overwrite or delete any version at any time.
limits: Every download hits one server and one disk, so billions of downloads a day are impossible
A maintainer can overwrite a version, so the same name and version can mean different code on different days
Deleting a version breaks every build that depends on it, as happened when a tiny popular package was removed in 2016
Resolving dependencies takes one request per package, so a build makes hundreds of round trips
Anyone with a stolen password can publish, and nothing shows where a package came from
Malware and look-alike names are published as easily as real packages

steps.title: Make every version immutable, and store tarballs by their hash
steps.problem: If a maintainer can replace the bytes behind 'colorize 1.1.5', two builds on different days can run different code under the same name, and nobody can reproduce or audit a build.
steps.fix: A version is written once. The publish API computes a SHA-256 hash of the tarball (a fingerprint of the file) and stores the file in object storage under that hash, so the storage is content-addressed. The metadata row for 'name@version' records the hash, and a second publish of the same name and version is refused unless the bytes are identical, in which case it does nothing. Clients get the expected hash along with the version and check it after every download. Names are first-come-first-served and a version number can be used only once, even if the first publish was removed.
steps.tradeoff: Builds are reproducible and any tampering with stored bytes is detectable. Maintainers cannot fix a typo in a published version and must publish a new one, which is why a registry needs yanking, and identical files shared by many versions are stored only once.

steps.title: Put the tarballs behind a CDN
steps.problem: Ten billion downloads a day would melt a single origin and make installs in distant regions slow.
steps.fix: Because a tarball URL names an immutable object, it can be cached forever: the CDN serves it with a one-year, immutable cache lifetime and the origin is only asked on a miss. Popular packages are hit almost always, so the hit rate for tarballs is above 98 percent and the origin sees a small fraction of the traffic. Several CDN providers or a tiered cache in front of the object store absorb a miss storm, and concurrent misses for the same object are collapsed into one origin request.
steps.tradeoff: Downloads are fast everywhere and the origin load is small, and the same URL gives the same bytes from any cache. A CDN is a third party that could be wrong or compromised, which is why the client still checks the hash, and the long tail of rarely used versions still goes to the origin.

steps.title: Serve dependency resolution from cached metadata documents
steps.problem: Picking versions that satisfy every range needs the dependencies of every candidate version, and asking the server one question per package gives hundreds of round trips and a heavy load on the database.
steps.fix: The registry publishes one metadata document per package that lists all its versions, their dependency ranges, hashes and flags such as yanked. The client downloads the documents it needs, usually from the CDN, and does the range resolution itself, then fetches the tarballs. A publish goes through a queue: an indexer updates the package's document in the metadata index and purges that one URL in the CDN, so the new version appears in about a minute. Documents are short-lived in the cache and use ETags, so a revalidation is cheap, and a lockfile records the exact result so later installs skip resolution.
steps.tradeoff: The registry does almost no work per install, resolution scales with the number of clients, and lockfile builds do not need the metadata at all. Documents of very popular packages are large, so a compact form is served, and a client can see a version a minute late.

steps.title: Authenticate publishers and record where a version came from
steps.problem: Anyone with a stolen token can publish a new version of a popular package, and a client has no way to know whether a tarball was built from the public source code.
steps.fix: Publishing needs a scoped token with two-factor authentication for people, or better, trusted publishing: the CI system proves its identity with a short-lived OIDC token (a signed proof of identity) and the registry accepts a publish only from the repository and workflow that the maintainer registered, so no long-lived secret exists. The build produces a signed attestation (a signed statement) of the source commit, the builder and the tarball hash. It is checked on publish and written to a public append-only transparency log, and clients can verify it before they install.
steps.tradeoff: A stolen password is no longer enough, and anyone can audit what built a package. Short-lived credentials and registered workflows take effort to set up, small maintainers must be able to publish without them, and an attestation shows where code was built, not that the code is good.

steps.title: Decide what yank and unpublish mean
steps.problem: A maintainer may want a bad version gone, but deleting a version that thousands of projects depend on breaks all of their builds, and keeping a dangerous one leaves everyone exposed.
steps.fix: Make deletion a policy, not a button. A yanked version is hidden from new resolution, so no fresh build picks it, but a project whose lockfile already names it can still download it. Deprecation adds a warning message. Unpublishing is allowed only in a short window after publish or when nothing depends on the package, and is otherwise refused. For malware or legal reasons the registry's security team can take a version down: the bytes are replaced by a tombstone (a marker that says the version was removed) and the version number stays reserved. Changes go through the publish queue so the metadata and the CDN are updated together.
steps.tradeoff: One maintainer's decision cannot break the world's builds, and an emergency takedown is still possible. A yanked bad version keeps running in the builds that locked it, and a tombstone makes those builds fail loudly on purpose, so the choice between safe and working is made case by case.

steps.title: Scan every publish, and watch for look-alike names
steps.problem: Attackers publish packages named like popular ones ('colorize' versus 'colorise'), packages that run code at install time, and new versions of stolen accounts' packages, and they are found only when someone gets hurt.
steps.fix: A new version goes to a scanner queue before it is released to the index. The scanner runs static rules and a sandboxed install, looking for network calls, credential reads, obfuscated code and install scripts, and compares the new version with the previous one. New names are compared with popular names by edit distance (how many letters differ) and common substitutions, and suspicious ones are held for review. Publishing is rate-limited for new accounts, and reports from users go to the same pipeline. A confirmed bad version is taken down as in the previous step.
steps.tradeoff: Many attacks are stopped in minutes, before anyone installs them. Scanning adds a delay to every publish, it can never catch everything, and false positives annoy honest maintainers, so most findings lower trust or hold a version instead of blocking it outright.

failures.scenario: A popular package releases a version and every CDN cache misses at once
failures.impact: Thousands of builds ask for the same new tarball in the same second and the origin and object store are flooded.
failures.answer: The CDN collapses concurrent misses for one URL into a single origin request, and a tiered cache means only one regional cache goes to the origin. The metadata document is purged at once, but the tarball is fetched on first demand. Rate limits and a small warm-up fetch after publish keep the origin steady.

failures.scenario: A maintainer's account is stolen and a malicious version is published
failures.impact: Every build that allows a range such as ^1.4.0 and has no lockfile pulls the malicious code within minutes.
failures.answer: Trusted publishing means a stolen password cannot publish, and a new version without the usual provenance is flagged. The scanner compares it with the last version and holds it. If it gets through, a report triggers a takedown with a tombstone, and the registry notifies projects that installed the version.

failures.scenario: The CDN, a mirror or the object store returns different bytes than were published
failures.impact: A corrupted or tampered tarball could be installed on millions of machines.
failures.answer: The metadata, which names the hash, is served separately from the tarball and can be signed. The client hashes every tarball and refuses one that does not match the hash in the lockfile or the metadata, and the object store verifies hashes on write and runs periodic scrubs of stored objects.

failures.impact: Publishes and fresh resolutions fail, and with them every build that needs a new package.
failures.answer: Tarballs and metadata keep being served from the CDN with stale-if-error, and lockfile builds need only tarballs, so most installs continue. Companies run a caching proxy of their own so that they have a copy of everything they have used. Publishing waits for the origin to return.

failures.scenario: A maintainer asks to delete a package that others depend on
failures.impact: If it is deleted, all builds that depend on it fail, and the name can be taken by someone else.
failures.answer: The request is refused for a package with dependents once it is past the short unpublish window, and the maintainer can deprecate or yank instead. A deleted name is reserved, so it cannot be re-registered to serve other code.

alternatives.title: Who resolves dependencies

options.name: The client, from cached metadata
options.pro: Almost no server work, cacheable, and works with a lockfile offline
options.con: Metadata documents are large, and every client needs the resolver

options.name: The server, per request
options.pro: Small responses and one place to improve the algorithm
options.con: CPU on the registry for every install, and hard to cache

alternatives.pick: The client resolves from cached metadata documents, with a lockfile.

alternatives.title: What unpublish means

options.name: Maintainer can delete any time
options.con: Breaks everyone's builds, and the name can be hijacked

options.name: Immutable, with yank and a narrow unpublish window
options.pro: Builds keep working and the name stays reserved
options.con: A bad version stays downloadable for those who locked it

options.name: Immutable, plus takedown for malware
options.pro: Dangerous bytes can be removed in an emergency
options.con: Needs a security team, and takedowns break builds on purpose

alternatives.pick: Immutable with yank, a narrow unpublish window, and takedown by the registry for malware.

alternatives.title: How tarballs are stored and named

options.name: By name and version
options.pro: Readable URLs and an easy mapping
options.con: The same name can hide different bytes if something goes wrong

options.name: By content hash
options.con: Needs an index from name and version to hash

alternatives.pick: Content-addressed storage, with a name-and-version index in the metadata.

alternatives.title: How publishes are signed

options.name: Long-lived maintainer keys
options.con: Keys get lost or stolen, and rotation is painful

options.name: Keyless: short-lived certificates from the CI identity
options.pro: No secret to steal, and the transparency log shows who published
options.con: Depends on the identity provider and on CI, and not every maintainer uses CI

alternatives.pick: Keyless signing for CI publishers, with a plain token and two-factor authentication still allowed.

quiz.question: A small registry stores each tarball as a file named after the package and version, and maintainers may upload again at any time. A maintainer fixes a typo by re-uploading 'fastjson 2.3.1'. Monday's CI run and Tuesday's CI run now install different code under the same version, and nobody can explain the diff. What is the best design change?
options: Allow overwrites only in the first 24 hours after the first publish, and make every later upload to that version number fail
Refuse a second upload of that name and version unless the bytes match, and keep the hash in metadata for clients to check
Keep each upload under a timestamped path, and let installs pick the file with the newest upload time for that version
Record file size and upload time in the metadata, so that clients can warn when a version has changed since their last build
quiz.explanation: A version that is written once and tied to a hash means the same name and version always gives the same bytes, and any change is detectable. A 24 hour window still lets bytes drift, so builds in that window stay irreproducible. A newest-upload rule keeps changing the code under one version, and recording size and time only warns after the damage.

quiz.question: A registry serves 10 billion tarball downloads a day. Assume peak traffic is 3 times the daily average, and the CDN hit rate for tarballs is 98 percent. The team asks how many requests per second the origin must be ready for at peak. Which answer is closest, and what should they do about it?
options: About 350,000 per second, because a CDN only reduces latency, so the origin must be sharded by hash to take that load
About 2,300 per second, from 2 percent of the average rate, so a fixed origin of that size is enough for the day
About 70 per second, because immutable files are fetched once per cache and then kept for the one-year cache lifetime
About 7,000 per second, so size for that and collapse concurrent misses for one URL into a single origin request
quiz.explanation: 10 billion a day is about 115,000 per second on average and about 350,000 at peak. A 2 percent miss rate leaves roughly 7,000 per second at the origin. Using the average instead of the peak gives 2,300, which would be too small exactly when it matters. A CDN cuts origin load, not only latency, so 350,000 is not the origin figure, and 70 per second ignores the many rarely used versions that miss.

quiz.question: A maintainer's stolen account published version 1.4.9 of a popular package 40 minutes ago. The security team confirms it steals cloud credentials. About 3,000 projects already have 1.4.9 in their lockfiles, and the unpublish window has long passed. What should the registry do now?
options: Take the version down: replace the bytes with a tombstone, keep the number reserved, and purge it from the index and CDN through the publish queue
Yank 1.4.9 so that new resolutions skip it, because projects with a lockfile need to keep downloading it to avoid broken builds
Overwrite 1.4.9 with the clean code from 1.4.8, so that every build that locked the version gets safe bytes without any failure
Delete the whole package and release the name, so that the maintainer can register it again after resetting the credentials
quiz.explanation: A malicious version must stop being downloadable, so the registry replaces it with a tombstone and keeps the number reserved. The locked builds then fail loudly, which is the intended trade. Yanking alone would leave those 3,000 projects still pulling the malware. Overwriting changes the bytes behind a version number, and releasing the name invites a new registration.
